## The idea

A dominant chord creates a strong expectation of a tonic a fifth below. A
*secondary dominant* points that expectation at a diatonic chord other than the
home tonic. The target sounds briefly promoted, as though a light has moved
onto it, then the progression continues in the original key.

In C major, the dominant of G is D major. D major contains F-sharp, which does
not belong to C major. That chromatic note is the audible signal. Write the
chord as V/V: the dominant of the dominant. The slash names the temporary
target rather than a permanent key change.

I hear the effect best in a comparison. Play a progression using the ordinary
diatonic ii chord, D minor, then replace it with D major before G. Keep rhythm,
voicing, and synth fixed.

## Run this

The first four bars remain diatonic. The second pass changes one chord quality.
Chord roots and qualities stay as data so the difference is visible.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :piano

diatonic = [
  {root: :c3, quality: :major},
  {root: :d3, quality: :minor},
  {root: :g2, quality: :major},
  {root: :c3, quality: :major}
]

tonicised = [
  {root: :c3, quality: :major},
  {root: :d3, quality: :major}, # V/V: F-sharp points toward G
  {root: :g2, quality: :major},
  {root: :c3, quality: :major}
]

define :play_progression do |chords|
  chords.each do |item|
    play_chord chord(item[:root], item[:quality]),
      release: 1.8,
      amp: 0.75
    sleep 2
  end
end

play_progression diatonic
sleep 2
play_progression tonicised
```

The D minor in the first pass continues gently to G. D major in the second pass
adds F-sharp, which pulls more sharply toward the G chord.

## Change one thing

1. Change the target G major to G minor in both arrays. The D major dominant now
   approaches a minor target. Listen for the retained root pull and the changed
   colour at resolution.
2. Change D major to D7 by setting quality to :dom7. The added C strengthens the
   dominant function because it forms a tritone with F-sharp. Compare the
   urgency with the plain triad.
3. Move the tonicised chord one position earlier, before D minor rather than G.
   The pitches remain available, but the expected target is denied. Listen for
   the chord sounding unexplained instead of directional.

## Why it works

The home key defines a set of diatonic chords. Secondary dominants temporarily
apply the dominant-tonic relation inside that set. Choose a target chord, find
the root a perfect fifth above it, and build a major triad or dominant seventh
there. At least one pitch will often come from outside the home scale.

Tonicisation is local. The target receives emphasis for a moment, but the
following chords still confirm the original tonic. A modulation lasts long
enough for the ear to adopt a new tonic and reorganise later Roman numerals
around it. Duration and follow-through separate these effects more than the
presence of a chromatic pitch does.

The slash notation behaves like a nested address. V/V asks for degree V in the
temporary context of degree V. In code, that can be resolved in two steps:
resolve the target root against the current key, then move seven semitones above
the target and construct a major or dominant-seventh chord.

Voice leading makes the chromatic pitch legible. In C major, F-sharp in D major
normally rises to G. Hide it in a distant octave or move it downward and the
tonicisation weakens even though the chord label remains V/V.

## Take it further

Write an eight-bar diatonic progression in one major key. Choose one non-tonic
diatonic chord and precede it with its own dominant. Render the original and
tonicised versions back to back from parallel data arrays. Label the target,
the slash numeral, and every chromatic pitch. The target sound is one clear
local arrival with the final bars confirming the original key.
